Moderna-Merck cancer vaccine success marks breakthrough for personalised mRNA treatment
Technology
Health & Fitness
24 Aug 2026 • 10:02 AM MYT
The Vibes
Featuring breaking news & latest stories from every side.
A PERSONALISED mRNA-based cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck & Co. has delivered a landmark result in a late-stage melanoma trial, strengthening hopes that technology originally propelled into the mainstream by Covid-19 vaccines could eventually become a powerful weapon against cancer.
The companies said the vaccine reduced the rate of melanoma recurrence in a final-stage clinical trial, marking the first time an mRNA-based cancer vaccine has demonstrated success in a large-scale study.
Bloomberg reported on Monday that although Moderna and Merck have yet to disclose the full results or the magnitude of the benefit, the announcement has been welcomed by investors and cancer researchers as a potentially significant turning point for a field that has struggled for decades to translate promising laboratory findings into successful human trials.
The findings could also reinvigorate interest in mRNA technology, which faced widespread scepticism during the Covid-19 pandemic and continues to attract criticism, including from US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Investors responded strongly to the announcement, with Moderna shares surging 177% on the day the results were reported.
Unlike conventional vaccines designed to prevent infectious diseases, personalised cancer vaccines are intended to treat people who already have cancer, particularly by reducing the risk of the disease returning after surgery.
The Moderna-Merck approach uses mRNA to instruct cells to produce fragments of mutated proteins, known as neoantigens, found in a patient’s tumour.
The immune system is then trained to recognise those mutations and mount an attack against cancer cells carrying them.
The technology is personalised because cancer mutations vary significantly from one patient to another, even among people diagnosed with the same type of cancer.
Scientists analyse a patient’s tumour sample and use an algorithm to identify mutations most likely to trigger an immune response. The resulting vaccine can contain up to 34 mutations selected specifically for that patient.
Jane Healy, head of oncology early development at Merck, said the number of mutations included in the vaccine provided multiple targets against the patient’s cancer.
“Thirty-four is quite a lot of chances, of shots on goal,” she said, adding that the approach was designed to cover “a sufficient amount of the spectrum of a patient’s cancer”.
The strategy differs from existing cancer treatments such as chemotherapy, targeted drugs and conventional immunotherapy.
Chemotherapy attacks rapidly dividing cells, while targeted medicines block specific proteins that drive cancer growth. Immunotherapy drugs such as Merck’s Keytruda work by disabling mechanisms that allow cancer cells to evade the immune system.
Personalised cancer vaccines instead aim to teach the immune system to identify the specific mutations carried by an individual patient’s tumour.
The approach is particularly suited to patients who have undergone surgery and are at high risk of recurrence, when the remaining cancer burden may be relatively small and more vulnerable to an immune response.
However, important questions surrounding the latest melanoma results remain unanswered.
The companies have not yet released detailed findings, including the size of the reduction in recurrence. Researchers also do not yet know whether patients receiving the vaccine will live longer.
The trial is continuing to collect longer-term data, with the full findings expected to be presented at an upcoming scientific meeting.
The success has nevertheless encouraged wider efforts to develop mRNA-based cancer treatments.
Moderna and Merck are testing their personalised approach in other cancers, including lung, bladder and kidney tumours.
Germany’s BioNTech and Switzerland’s Roche are also developing personalised mRNA cancer vaccines targeting diseases including pancreatic and colon cancer.
BioNTech is separately pursuing a standardised mRNA vaccine approach for patients with advanced lung cancer and head and neck cancer.
Beyond cancer, researchers are also exploring mRNA technology for rare and metabolic diseases, with Moderna testing treatments for propionic acidemia and methylmalonic acidemia.
The latest melanoma findings do not establish mRNA vaccines as a cure for cancer, but they provide some of the strongest clinical evidence yet that the technology can be adapted to train the immune system against an individual patient’s tumour.
For cancer researchers, the results could represent an important step towards making personalised vaccines a practical part of cancer treatment rather than a long-standing scientific ambition. - August 24, 2026

Drugs & Therapies.content: Hanmi Pharmaceutical(128940) is drawing market attention to the supply price ahead of the launch of its independently developed obesity treatment “Effe” (EPPE, ingredient name Efpeglenatide). The glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1 obesity drug market, which changed the paradigm of obesity treatment, is currently dominated by “Wegovy” from the Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk and “Mounjaro” from the U.S. drugmaker Eli Lilly and Company. Attention is on whether the arrival of the first domestically developed GLP-1 obesity treatment will trigger price competition and whether global drugmakers will actually respond on price. ◇ Lilly and Novo on alert over Effe price According to the pharmaceutical industry on the 24th, Hanmi Pharmaceutical’s new obesity drug Effe is expected to be launched by the end of the year at the latest. Effe was designated for Global Innovative product Fast Track (GIFT), under which the Ministery of Food and Drug Safety prioritizes and shortens the review of innovative new drugs. Considering the procedure, there is an expectation that approval could come around Oct. The company also said, “If approval is granted, we plan to launch the product as early as Oct. or by the end of the year at the latest.” Following the launch timing of Effe, the focus of the medical community and securities market is on how much lower its launch price will be than Mounjaro and Wegovy, which split the domestic market. Non-reimbursable drugs, which are not covered by national health insurance, do not have prices set based on insurance list prices like reimbursable drugs. Currently, new obesity drugs are non-reimbursable, so patients must pay the full price, and the burden varies by medical institution and prescribing conditions. Because obesity often requires long-term treatment, a monthly price difference of tens of thousands of won can feel significant to patients. According to a domestic healthcare platform’s tally, the average price per pack of Mounjaro by dose at pharmacies in Seoul was △2.5 mg 300,500 won, △5 mg 394,210 won, △7.5 mg 547,100 won, △10 mg 546,010 won, △12.5 mg 699,730 won, and △15 mg 701,780 won. The average hospital consultation fee was 21,570 won. Wegovy is priced from the low 200,000-won range per month to around 400,000 won depending on dose. Some in the industry expect Effe’s price could be set at about half of Mounjaro’s initial monthly dose price in the 300,000-won range. Others note that, given research and development investment expense, production costs, and revenue considerations, pricing in the 100,000-won range will be difficult. Korean subsidiaries of global drugmakers with obesity drugs are closely watching Hanmi Pharmaceutical’s strategy. Effe’s price and market response could also affect the pricing policies of Wegovy and Mounjaro. An industry official said, “Because Effe’s price could influence pricing policies for existing Asian markets and global obesity drugs beyond the domestic market, Eli Lilly and Company and Novo Nordisk are also on high alert.” Hanmi Pharmaceutical has also made price competitiveness a key battleground. Compared with Wegovy and Mounjaro, which are imported as finished goods from overseas, the company plans to leverage its domestic manufacturing base to secure the market with strengths in price and supply stability. However, Hanmi Pharmaceutical says it has not yet decided on Effe’s price. It is understood that there are differing views on the pricing strategy even among group executives. Because the rival’s follow-up response after Effe’s launch must also be considered, there is caution about the pricing strategy leaking early. A shift in strategies at Eli Lilly and Company and Novo Nordisk following Effe’s launch is also a key point to watch. An industry official said, “Once Effe launches, Wegovy and Mounjaro will ultimately move to cut prices as well.” ◇ “Treatment effect” matters as much as price In the pharmaceutical market, competitiveness is not determined by price alone. The most important criteria for patients and clinicians when choosing a drug are treatment effect and side effects. Wegovy and Mounjaro have an advantage in that they have already accumulated extensive prescribing experience and clinical data in the global market. However, weight-loss effects vary by patient, and there are also a growing number of cases in which treatment is discontinued due to expense burdens, bodily reactions, and side effects. Hanmi Pharmaceutical expressed confidence based on safety and treatment experience confirmed in clinical data on Korean patients. According to the company, in a phase 3 trial of 448 Korean adult patients with obesity, the Efpeglenatide group showed an average 9.75% weight loss from baseline after 40 weeks. In the treatment group, 79% lost at least 5% of their weight, and about half lost 10% or more. Wegovy (semaglutide) from Novo Nordisk showed an average 14.9% weight loss in a representative 68-week trial, and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) from Eli Lilly and Company showed an average 16.0% to 22.5% weight loss by dose in a 72-week trial. Because treatment duration, patient composition, and other trial conditions differ across studies for each therapy, there are limits to simply comparing weight loss effects. Hanmi Pharmaceutical said that, compared with other obesity drug clinical data, gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as vomiting and nausea were relatively fewer or milder. Effe applies the “LAPSCOVERY” technology, which allows the drug to be released slowly to maintain efficacy longer. The company is also pursuing a strategy of combining with digital therapeutic solutions. This targets the shift in obesity treatment from short-term weight reduction to long-term weight management and lifestyle improvement. Ultimately, observers say Effe’s successful market entry depends on how quickly it can win the choices of clinicians and patients in a domestic market preoccupied by global big pharma. ☞ GLP-1 obesity drugs GLP-1 is a hormone secreted in the intestines after meals that acts on the brain’s appetite control center to increase satiety and reduce appetite. At the same time, it slows gastric emptying to keep food in the stomach longer and promotes insulin secretion from the pancreas to help control blood sugar. GLP-1 obesity treatments mimic or enhance these GLP-1 actions to reduce food intake and induce weight loss.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Hanmi Pharm Signs Exclusive Licensing Deal with Genentech for Novel Obesity Therapy - PR Newswire
Drugs & Therapies.content:
HM17321, a proprietary UCN2 (urocortin-2) analog, is being developed as a treatment for chronic-weight management and associated conditions, including obesity
Total deal value of up to $2.3 billion, including upfront, milestone payments and tiered royalties based on net sales
SEOUL, South Korea
,
Aug. 24, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- Hanmi Pharm announced today that it has entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of Hanmi's novel metabolic treatment candidate, HM17321 (UCN2), for obesity and associated conditions such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, worldwide. The agreement excludes South Korea.
HM17321 is a proprietary UCN2 (urocortin-2) analog with a non-incretin mechanism of action and represents a potential first-in-class treatment designed to simultaneously promote weight loss and preserve lean body mass. In contrast, while existing
GLP-1
based incretin therapies have demonstrated meaningful weight reduction, these therapies are associated with a reduction in lean body mass.
In preclinical studies, HM17321 has shown both quantitative and qualitative improvements in weight reduction when used as a monotherapy and in combination with
GLP-1
-based therapies. Furthermore, as a peptide-based therapeutic, HM17321 may have future potential for use in fixed-dose combination (FDC) products or combination regimens with incretin-based treatments.
In November 2025, Hanmi received IND (Investigational New Drug) clearance from the U.S. FDA (Food and Drug Administration) to initiate a Phase 1 clinical trial of HM17321. The ongoing clinical study is evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of HM17321 in healthy volunteers and individuals with obesity.
Hanmi will be responsible for completing the Phase 1 clinical trial, after which Genentech will take over development starting with Phase 2 clinical trials.
In-Young Choi, Senior Executive Vice President, Head of R&D Division of Hanmi Pharm stated, "The paradigm of obesity treatment is evolving beyond simple weight reduction toward improving body composition and restoring metabolic health. We are very pleased that the differentiated scientific mechanism and development potential of HM17321 have been recognized by the global market. Hanmi Pharm will continue to dedicate its efforts to developing innovative medicines that can deliver more fundamental and differentiated therapeutic value to patients."
"With our growing cardiometabolic pipeline and strong diagnostic expertise, Roche is advancing a portfolio designed to meet the diverse needs of people living with obesity and related health conditions," said Boris L. Zaïtra, head of Roche Corporate Business Development. "By licensing this next-generation investigational therapy with first-in-class potential from Hanmi, Roche and Genentech will pursue a differentiated approach to selectively reduce fat mass while improving both muscle mass and muscle function. We look forward to further developing this medicine in order to address important unmet needs for people living with obesity and other metabolic diseases."
Under the terms of the agreement, Hanmi will receive an upfront payment of USD 190 million from Genentech. Including development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, the total deal value could reach approximately USD 2.3 billion. In addition, Hanmi will be eligible to receive tiered royalties on future product sales following commercialization.
SOURCE Hanmi Pharm. Co., Ltd.

사진 확대
A panoramic view of Hanmi Pharmaceutical's headquarters. [HANMI Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.]
Hanmi Pharmaceutical has decided to transfer its technology to "Genentech," a subsidiary of Roche Group, for up to $2.3 billion (about 3.1723 trillion won).
This is the largest-ever single candidate material export by a domestic pharmaceutical and bio company to global big pharma, and Hanmi Pharmaceutical is also the largest single-material contract with Sanofi in 2015.
Hanmi Pharmaceutical announced on the 24th that it has signed an exclusive license agreement for its new drug candidate HM17321. If you include future clinical development, regulatory approval, and commercialization milestones in advance of $190 million (about 262.1 billion won), it will be worth up to $2.3 billion. The company said it will also receive separate royalties after the launch of the product.
Under the contract, Genentech has exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize HM17321 in markets worldwide except Korea. Hanmi Pharmaceutical will complete the ongoing phase 1 clinical trial, and Genentech will lead the development of the phase 2 clinical trial.
HM17321 is a non-Incretin-based UCN2 (Eurocortin-2) analogue developed by Hanmi Pharmaceutical. It is aiming for a new 'first-in-class' drug that simultaneously implements weight loss and muscle preservation. In the case of existing glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1)-based obesity treatments, it has been pointed out as a limitation that despite the significant weight loss effect, the amount of fat such as muscles decreases together during the treatment process.
According to Hanmi Pharmaceutical, HM17321 showed excellent results in weight loss and body composition improvement in non-clinical studies not only when administered alone but also in combination with GLP-1 treatment. It is also developed based on peptides and has the advantage of expanding the area of combination treatment with a fixed-dose complex (FDC) with incremental drugs in the future.
Currently, Hanmi Pharmaceutical received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in November last year for the phase 1 clinical trial plan (IND) of HM17321 and is evaluating safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in healthy adult and obese patients.
Choi In-young, vice president of Hanmi Pharmaceutical, said, "The obesity treatment paradigm is evolving beyond simple weight loss to improve body composition and restore metabolic health. The differentiated scientific mechanism and potential of HM17321 have been recognized in the global market."
Boris L. Zeitra Roche, head of corporate business development, also said, "We plan to pursue a differentiated treatment strategy that selectively reduces fat mass while improving muscle mass and muscle function."

Pharma Industry.content:
Taiwan's TAHO Pharmaceuticals' Antithrombotic Oral Film Clears FDA Acceptance Hurdle, Targets World's Second-Largest Drug Market
Add to Google Preferred Sources
TAHO Pharmaceuticals, a Taiwanese emerging biotech company, announced that its antithrombotic oral film drug BEQIA has officially entered substantive review by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as of August 21. BEQIA is the world's first Apixaban antithrombotic oral film, developed using the company's proprietary TDS (Transepithelial Delivery System) platform, targeting elderly patients and those with swallowing difficulties. The originator drug Eliquis posted U.S. sales of $29.2 billion in 2025. Despite government-mandated price cuts under the Inflation Reduction Act, the lower prices have paradoxically driven a surge in new prescriptions. IQVIA projects the U.S. market to reach $28 billion this year, solidifying its position as the world's second-largest drug. TAHO Pharmaceuticals has already signed confidentiality agreements with dozens of pharmaceutical companies across Europe, the U.S., Australia/New Zealand, Latin America, and Asia, entering substantive licensing negotiations. The subsequent approval timeline and licensing progress will be key operational indicators to watch.
Key Elements
TAHO Pharmaceuticals
BEQIA
Apixaban
Eliquis
Bristol Myers Squibb
Pfizer
U.S. Food and Drug Administration
TDS Transepithelial Delivery System
IQVIA
TAHO Pharmaceuticals (6467.TW), a Taiwanese emerging biotech company listed on the Taipei Exchange, has achieved a critical milestone in the development of its novel antithrombotic formulation. The company announced that the New Drug Application (NDA) for its oral film drug BEQIA (TAH3311) officially entered substantive review by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 21 (U.S. time), marking a significant step toward product approval and subsequent global commercialization.
TAHO Pharmaceuticals stated that it resubmitted the NDA for BEQIA to the FDA on June 19 (U.S. time). Since that date coincided with a U.S. federal holiday, the FDA's official receipt date was June 22. According to a notification letter issued by the FDA on July 14, if no incomplete application notice was received within 60 days of submission, the case would enter substantive review on August 21. As of August 21 (U.S. time), the company had not received any such notification, confirming that it has cleared the acceptance threshold and formally entered substantive review.
BEQIA is the world's first Apixaban antithrombotic oral film, developed by TAHO Pharmaceuticals using its proprietary TDS (Transepithelial Delivery System) platform technology. The originator drug for Apixaban, marketed under the brand name Eliquis, was co-developed by Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) and Pfizer, and is the world's largest small-molecule drug. More than 70% of the drug's usage is for atrial fibrillation patients to prevent blood clot formation.
According to IQVIA data, the originator drug Eliquis achieved U.S. sales of $29.2 billion (approximately NT$930 billion) in 2025. Notably, the drug was subject to government-mandated price reductions in 2025 under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), with prices cut from $8–10 per tablet (approximately NT$320) to $5.65 (approximately NT$180), and further to $3.85 (approximately NT$120). The market had initially expected a significant decline in revenue this year.
However, BMS's financial report showed that Eliquis generated global revenue of $4.481 billion (approximately NT$140 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, up 22% year-over-year. The counterintuitive revenue growth was primarily driven by the price cuts, which led to a substantial increase in new prescriptions as patients who should have been taking the medication could now afford it. Insurance companies pay $2,772 for a full year of medication, which is far less than the $46,700 annual care cost that would be incurred in the event of a stroke. IQVIA further projects that the drug's revenue will grow significantly by 20% to 25% this year, with the U.S. market reaching $28 billion (approximately NT$890 billion), firmly securing its position as the world's second-largest drug, behind only Keytruda and ahead of Ozempic.
TAHO Pharmaceuticals has clearly identified its target market pain points. A survey by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) indicates that the number of atrial fibrillation patients in the U.S. reached 10.55 million in 2025, with patients aged 65 and older accounting for 75% of the total. Among these elderly patients, approximately half experience swallowing difficulties. BEQIA's oral film formulation addresses the clinical limitations of current tablet forms, which require water for administration and present challenges with crushing and swallowing, while also reducing choking risks and lowering the incidence of aspiration pneumonia.
With the entry into FDA substantive review, TAHO Pharmaceuticals' global commercial licensing collaborations are simultaneously gaining momentum. The company stated that BEQIA is advancing global market licensing partnerships in parallel to accelerate the product's commercialization timeline. To date, the company has attracted dozens of pharmaceutical companies across Europe, the U.S., Australia/New Zealand, Latin America, and Asia to sign confidentiality agreements, entering substantive licensing negotiations.
Industry observers noted that TAHO Pharmaceuticals has already received approval for its listing, and if BEQIA successfully obtains U.S. drug approval, it would represent a critical inflection point for the company's transition from R&D to commercialization. The subsequent approval timeline and licensing negotiation outcomes will serve as key indicators for the market to monitor TAHO Pharmaceuticals' operational performance.

Pharma Industry.content:
Now 'quality' competition rather than weight loss
Food intake is maintained, but weight loss is lost by increasing energy consumption
사진 확대
"Please draw an image of losing weight by eating a lot and exercising." An image created by AI. [Gemini]
With the obesity treatment craze sweeping the world, the pharmaceutical bio industry has already begun the next generation of drug competition. Unlike the GLP-1 family, which suppresses appetite, "obesity treatment 2.0" aims to lose weight by increasing energy consumption while maintaining the amount of meals. Attention is focusing on whether it will be an alternative to those who suffer side effects such as Hugo Bee and Mountaineer.
The core of obesity treatment 2.0 is a 'healthy diet'. Since the amount of meals is maintained, there are no side effects of the gastrointestinal tract such as nausea, and muscle mass does not decrease. Instead, it burns more unnecessary fat to use more energy. It is a new diet strategy that can only select and lose fat in our body.
According to a recent UC Berkeley study, the low-molecular compound "TOFA" has been shown to reduce weight by increasing energy consumption in the body. As a result of administering TOFA to obese mice for four weeks, the researchers lost about 18% of their average weight.
It should be noted that there was no significant change in the amount of intake even after administration of TOFA, and the weight lost was mainly body fat. It is differentiated from the loss of muscles by reducing the amount of obesity treatments currently used, such as Hugo Bee and Mountaineer. According to a meta-analysis of GLP-1 drugs conducted last year, about 25% of the weight lost from drug treatment was due to muscle loss.
Mice administered TOFA had an approximately 18% increase in energy consumption than usual in a temperature-23-degree environment. The amount of activity remained the same, but even if I stayed still, I burned more fat to create energy. This means that the metabolism of the cell itself has increased. It is a way to eat food as usual, keep your muscles, and lose only unnecessary fat.
Even if you stop administering it Phenomena' was much less than conventional obesity treatments. Since there was no change in food intake, there was no weight rebound even if treatment was stopped. The researchers explained, "Suspending GLP-1 drugs increases weight immediately and steeply, but TOFA drugs did not rebound significantly."
Since Hugo Bee and Mountaineero hit the pharmaceutical bio industry around the world, research on second-generation obesity treatments has been actively conducted in academia since last year. Academia has already found a number of candidate substances, and some are even conducting clinical trials with pharmaceutical companies.
Eolo Pharma, a Uruguay-based pharmaceutical company, developed a candidate substance for an obesity treatment called "SANA" last year with local university researchers. Last year, the Nature Sisters published the results of phase 1 clinical trials in humans, and it was found that they lost about 3% of their weight within 15 days of administration. It has proven both safety and drug effectiveness.
SANA's principle is to burn more fat while maintaining food intake. SANA causes mitochondria in adipocytes to consume more energy. If TOFA is the way to make less fat and burn more fat, SANA focuses all its power on fat burning.
These 'energy-consumption' obesity treatments are already entering the clinical development stage of the pharmaceutical bio industry. In the same way, HU6, an oral candidate being developed by Rivers Pharmaceuticals, an American biotechnology company, encourages more energy consumption. The goal is to minimize muscle loss by using fat as a major energy source. Currently, phase 2 clinical trials have been conducted for patients with obesity and metabolic diseases.
The competition standard for next-generation obesity treatments is shifting from the amount of weight loss to the quality. It's not just about how many kilograms you lost, it's about how much fat you lose and how much you preserve your muscles. Experts are also looking at ways to combine the "less eating" method and the "burning more fat" method in the future.
Researchers at UC Berkeley, who studied TOFA, said, "When combined with existing obesity treatments, it can induce greater weight loss," adding, "It is a strategy to maintain food intake control and metabolic health recovery." SANA researchers also said, "The GLP-1 family has made important progress in treating obesity, but it still needs to be supplemented. Measures to minimize muscle loss and weight rebound should be added."

Pharma Industry.content:
Four Briefings to Be Held in September, Each for a Different Participant Group
The Financial Supervisory Service announced on August 24 that it will hold four briefing sessions next month to ensure the smooth implementation of improved guidelines that require pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies to disclose objective grounds for clinical trial success rates and past development records.
The briefing sessions will be held on September 1 for KOSDAQ-listed companies (by KOSDAQ Association), September 8 for underwriters (at the Korea Institute of Financial Investment), September 15 for pre-IPO companies (at the Korea Institute of Financial Investment), and September 21 for KOSPI-listed companies (at the 2nd floor auditorium of the Financial Supervisory Service). During each session, the background and key improvements of the comprehensive pharmaceutical and biotechnology disclosure improvement plan will be introduced, as well as specific writing methods and important notes to help companies faithfully apply these standards to their disclosure work.
The comprehensive improvement plan for pharmaceutical and biotechnology disclosures, which was released last month, requires companies in these sectors to provide detailed grounds for public offering price calculations during the initial public offering (IPO) process and to transparently release information on research and development (R&D) status and product development history. The main goal is to prevent so-called 'inflated disclosures' and curb the practice of luring investors with rosy promotional phrases about 'dream new drugs.'
View original image
The Financial Supervisory Service stated that it will provide thorough guidance through these briefing sessions to ensure that pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies fully understand the improved disclosure standards. Furthermore, by preventing the submission of incomplete disclosure documents, the agency aims to minimize the work burden and funding schedule delays caused by correction requests by explaining each guideline item in detail.
Regarding fundraising, the agency will present detailed standards for core assumptions used when calculating public offering prices, thereby minimizing trial and error during the preparation of securities registration statements. Additionally, it plans to provide concrete methods for applying the newly introduced disclosure standards, so that companies can continue to deliver consistent and faithful information to investors even after listing.

Pharma Industry.content:
New Delhi [India], August 22:
In today’s global pharmaceutical and biotechnology landscape, the ability to make fast, confident, and well-informed decisions is no longer a competitive advantage — it is a baseline requirement for survival.
For India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, this reality is particularly acute. India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries are scaling at pace, driven by growing domestic demand, expanding export obligations, and increasing pressure to meet the quality and compliance standards of the world’s most stringent regulatory markets. At the same time, the volume, velocity, and complexity of R&D (research and development) data that organizations must manage has grown significantly.
Yet for many organizations, the systems designed to capture, manage, and surface that data have not kept pace. Research findings sit on disconnected platforms. Operational insights are buried in siloed workflows. And the leaders responsible for making portfolio, investment, and compliance decisions are often working from incomplete, delayed, or unverified information.
The consequences are significant. Slow decisions cost time and money. Decisions made on unreliable data carry strategic and regulatory risk. And in a market where speed-to-market, compliance confidence, and R&D productivity are defining competitive differentiators, the inability to access timely and trusted insights is a liability that compounds over time.
The organizations best positioned to lead in this environment share a common characteristic: they have moved beyond fragmented, point-in-time data access toward integrated information frameworks — connected digital ecosystems that give decision-makers consistent, reliable, and real-time visibility across their R&D and operational landscape.
This is the era of data-driven decision-making. And for India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, the question is no longer whether to build that capability, but how quickly it can be done.
The Challenge of Disconnected Information Systems
The challenge facing most pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations today is not a shortage of data. It is a shortage of accessible, connected, and trustworthy data that is available at the moment when decisions need to be made.
Across India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, organizations have invested significantly in digital solutions over the past decade. Electronic laboratory notebooks, laboratory information management systems, analytical platforms, regulatory submission systems, and enterprise resource planning platforms have all found their place in the modern R&D and manufacturing environment. Each was implemented to solve a specific problem. Each, in isolation, does.
But the cumulative effect of deploying multiple disconnected point solutions is a fragmented information landscape that works against the very decision-making it was designed to support.
Consider what this looks like in practice:
A
portfolio review meeting
is delayed because the data needed to assess program progress sits across three separate systems — none of which speak to each other
A
regulatory submission
requires manual reconciliation of records from multiple solutions, introducing both delay and the risk of inconsistency
A
quality investigation
takes days rather than hours because audit trails are incomplete, metadata is missing, and experimental context has been lost in translation between systems
A
senior leadership team
makes resource allocation decisions based on reports that are days or weeks old — because real-time visibility across the R&D pipeline simply does not exist
These are not edge cases. For many Indian pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations operating across multiple sites, managing collaborative R&D partnerships, and serving regulated markets in the US, EU, and beyond, this is the daily operational reality.
The operational cost of information fragmentation is well documented across the global pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, from lost R&D productivity to delayed regulatory submissions and slower time-to-market. For India’s generics and biosimilar manufacturers, where speed-to-market, regulatory confidence, and operational efficiency are existential competitive factors, the cost of information fragmentation is not an abstract concern. It is a measurable drag on performance, competitiveness, and growth.
Designing Systems That Support Strategic Decisions
Addressing the challenge of disconnected information is not simply a technology problem. It is a strategic design challenge which requires organizations to rethink not just the solutions they use, but the principles that govern how R&D data is captured, connected, and made available across the enterprise.
The organizations that have made the most progress in this area share a common architectural philosophy: data should flow freely, be trusted completely, and be accessible consistently — from the bench to the boardroom.
In practice, this means moving away from collections of point solutions toward integrated information frameworks built on four foundational principles:
1. Unified Data Architecture
A single, consistent data model that eliminates the need for manual translation, reformatting, or reconciliation between systems. When every team — chemistry, biology, formulation, regulatory, quality — works within the same data environment, information retains its context, its integrity, and its traceability from the moment it is created to the moment it informs a decision. This is particularly critical for organizations managing biologics registration workflows, where data integrity across the development lifecycle is a regulatory requirement.
2. End-to-End Workflow Continuity
Decision-making is only as good as the data that feeds it. When workflows are continuous — when the R&D lifecycle operates as a connected whole rather than a series of disconnected handoffs — leaders gain access to a complete, unbroken picture of program progress, experimental outcomes, and operational performance. This is the foundation of a true collaborative R&D environment.
3. AI-Ready Data Infrastructure
The next frontier of decision support in pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries is artificial intelligence (AI) in R&D — from predictive analytics and pattern recognition to automated summarization and semantic search. The role of artificial intelligence in knowledge management is increasingly central to how organizations surface insights, connect historical data, and accelerate decision-making across complex research programs. But AI is only as powerful as the data it operates on. Organizations that build connected, structured, and traceable data foundations today are positioning themselves to extract exponentially greater value from AI-enabled decision software solutions tomorrow.
4. Security and Compliance by Design
For organizations operating in regulated markets — and for India’s exporters, that means virtually every major market in the world — compliance cannot be an afterthought. Integrated information frameworks must embed audit readiness, data integrity controls, and intellectual property protection as foundational capabilities, not bolt-on features.
This is the design philosophy behind Signals One
TM
by Revvity Signals. As a unified, cloud-native solution spanning the entire R&D lifecycle, Signals One was built specifically to address the information fragmentation challenge that limits decision-making across pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations. By connecting scientific workflows, standardizing data architecture, and embedding AI-ready infrastructure across the R&D continuum, Signals One gives organizations the integrated information foundation that modern strategic decision-making demands.
For India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors — where the pressure to deliver quality, speed, and compliance simultaneously has never been greater — this kind of integrated instrument capability across the full research environment is not a future aspiration. It is a present-day strategic requirement.
The Strategic Benefits of Integrated Decision-Making
Organizations that make the transition from fragmented point solutions to integrated information frameworks do not simply solve an operational problem. They unlock a set of strategic capabilities that compound in value over time.
Faster, More Confident Decisions
When leaders have consistent, real-time access to reliable data across the R&D and operational landscape, decision cycles compress. Portfolio reviews that once required days of data preparation can be conducted with current information. Resource allocation decisions can be made with confidence rather than approximation. And the time between scientific insight and strategic action — one of the most critical intervals in the competitive pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries — shortens measurably.
For India’s generics and biosimilar manufacturers, where regulatory filing timelines and speed-to-market are direct drivers of commercial performance, faster and more confident decision-making translates directly into competitive advantage.
Reduced Strategic and Regulatory Risk
Decisions made on incomplete, inconsistent, or unverified data carry risk — both strategic and regulatory. Integrated information frameworks reduce that risk by ensuring that the data informing decision is complete, traceable, and audit-ready at every stage of the R&D process.
For organizations operating under the scrutiny of the US FDA, EMA, and other major regulatory bodies, as the majority of India’s pharmaceutical exporters do, this is not a marginal benefit. It is a fundamental risk management capability that protects both compliance, standing, and commercial reputation.
Stronger Long-Term Planning and Portfolio Intelligence
When data flows continuously and consistently across the R&D lifecycle, organizations accumulate something more valuable than individual data points — they build institutional knowledge. Historical experimental data becomes searchable and reusable. A well-structured compound management system ensures that research assets are tracked, accessible, and reusable across teams and programs. Patterns across programs become visible. And the intelligence needed to make long-term portfolio decisions becomes grounded in evidence rather than intuition.
Operational Efficiency at Scale
The operational benefits of integration — reduced manual data handling, eliminated reformatting, streamlined audit preparation, and seamless lab instrument integration — translate directly into cost efficiency and capacity. Research teams spend less time managing systems and more time advancing science. Quality and regulatory teams spend less time reconstructing records and more time ensuring compliance. And leadership teams spend less time waiting for information and more time acting on it.
India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations are scaling rapidly, expanding capacity, entering new markets and managing growing complexity simultaneously. This shifting landscape means that operational efficiency is not just a cost saving; it is the foundation for sustainable, scalable growth.
Building the Foundation for India’s Next Chapter
India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors are at an inflection point. The ambition is clear — to move up the value chain, to compete on quality and compliance as well as cost, and to strengthen India’s position as a trusted supplier to the world’s most demanding pharmaceutical markets.
Realizing this ambition requires more than a scientific talent and manufacturing scale. It requires the digital infrastructure to turn R&D data into decisions that can be made quickly, confidently, and consistently. Organizations that continue to rely on fragmented, disconnected systems will find that the operational and strategic costs of doing so grow alongside the complexity of their business.
The path forward is integration. Connected, AI-ready, compliance-embedded software solutions that support collaborative R&D at every level of the enterprise are no longer the preserve of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies. They are increasingly accessible — and increasingly necessary — for any organization serious about competing in global pharmaceutical and biotechnology markets.
For India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology leaders, the strategic priority is straightforward: build the information foundation that supports faster decisions, stronger compliance, and sustainable growth. The organizations that do so now will be better positioned to lead as the demands of global markets continue to evolve.
The era of data-driven decision-making is already here. The question for India’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology leaders is simple: is your R&D infrastructure ready to support it?
To learn more about how Revvity Signals can help your organization build the integrated information foundation for data-driven decision-making, contact us today.

Silicone Tubing for Pharmaceutical Transfer Market to Reach Index 190 by 2035 on Single-Use Bioprocessing Demand
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global
Silicone Tubing for Pharmaceutical Transfer market
, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global silicone tubing for pharmaceutical transfer market is entering a phase of sustained expansion, underpinned by the accelerating adoption of single-use technologies in biopharmaceutical manufacturing. As drug developers prioritize flexibility, contamination control, and cost efficiency, silicone tubing has become a critical consumable in fluid handling across upstream and downstream processes. The market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of approximately 6.8% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 190 by 2035 relative to 2025. This growth is driven by the rising production of biologics, including monoclonal antibodies and cell and gene therapies, which require high-purity, sterilizable tubing for safe and reliable fluid transfer. Platinum-cured silicone tubing, known for its superior biocompatibility and low extractable levels, continues to dominate demand, accounting for roughly 65% of value sales. Supply chain dynamics are shifting as manufacturers expand cleanroom capacity in Asia-Pacific to serve regional biopharma hubs, reducing lead times and enhancing supply resilience. However, qualification cycles of 9-15 months and stringent regulatory requirements remain barriers to rapid supplier diversification. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of market size, demand structure, trade flows, pricing, and competitive landscape, offering actionable insights for manufacturers, distributors, and investors through 2035.
The baseline scenario for the silicone tubing for pharmaceutical transfer market points to steady growth through 2035, supported by structural demand from biopharmaceutical manufacturing and laboratory research. The market is expected to expand at a CAGR of 6.8% over the forecast period, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to 190 by 2035. This growth is anchored in the continued shift toward single-use bioprocessing systems, which reduce cross-contamination risks and improve operational flexibility. Demand for platinum-cured tubing will remain robust, driven by its low leachability and compatibility with sensitive biologic products. The cell and gene therapy segment is projected to grow at over 10% annually, reflecting the increasing number of clinical trials and commercial therapies requiring sterile fluid paths. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will emerge as the fastest-growing region, with biopharma investments in China, India, and Southeast Asia boosting local production and consumption. North America and Europe will maintain significant shares, driven by established biopharma clusters and stringent regulatory standards. Supply-side dynamics include capacity expansions by key manufacturers and a growing emphasis on documentation and validation services. Challenges such as raw material price volatility and regulatory divergence across pharmacopoeias will persist, but overall, the market is poised for resilient growth as biopharmaceutical innovation continues to accelerate.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
Increasing adoption of single-use bioprocessing systems in biopharmaceutical manufacturing
Rising production of biologics, including monoclonal antibodies and recombinant proteins
Growth of cell and gene therapy workflows requiring sterile fluid handling
Stringent regulatory standards for contamination control and biocompatibility
Expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity in emerging markets
Technological advancements in platinum-cured silicone tubing with lower extractables
Potential Growth Constraints
Raw material price volatility linked to silicon metal and energy costs
Long qualification cycles (9-15 months) for new suppliers, limiting supply chain diversification
Regulatory divergence across pharmacopoeias (e.g., USP, EP, ChP) increasing compliance costs
High capital investment required for cleanroom manufacturing and validation infrastructure
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
Bioprocessing and Drug Manufacturing (estimated share: 45%)
This segment accounts for the largest share of silicone tubing demand, driven by the expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity worldwide. Silicone tubing is essential for transferring media, buffers, and active ingredients in upstream and downstream processes, including fermentation, cell culture, and purification. The shift toward single-use technologies is a key demand-side indicator, as manufacturers replace stainless steel systems with disposable fluid paths to reduce cleaning validation and cross-contamination risks. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from increasing investments in biologics production, particularly for monoclonal antibodies and biosimilars. The demand for platinum-cured tubing with low extractable profiles is rising, as regulatory scrutiny on leachables intensifies. Major companies are expanding their cleanroom capacity to meet the growing need for high-purity tubing, with a focus on documentation and validation support. The trend toward continuous manufacturing and intensified bioprocessing will further drive demand for robust, sterilizable tubing solutions. Current trend: Dominant segment, growing steadily with biologics production.
Major trends:
Adoption of single-use bioprocessing bags and tubing assemblies, Increasing demand for platinum-cured tubing with low extractables, Expansion of biopharma manufacturing capacity in Asia-Pacific, and Integration of tubing with sensors and connectors for automated processes.
Representative participants:
Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, Watson-Marlow Fluid Technology Group, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Parker Hannifin, and Freudenberg Medical.
Cell and Gene Therapy Workflows (estimated share: 20%)
Cell and gene therapy (CGT) represents a high-growth application for silicone tubing, as these therapies require sterile, closed-system fluid handling to maintain cell viability and prevent contamination. The segment is driven by the increasing number of clinical trials and commercial approvals for CAR-T therapies, gene therapies, and other personalized medicines. Silicone tubing is used in cell culture, harvesting, and formulation processes, where biocompatibility and low leachability are critical. The demand for single-use assemblies, including tubing with connectors and clamps, is rising as manufacturers adopt closed processing systems to comply with good manufacturing practices. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from the scaling up of CGT manufacturing, with a focus on automation and process intensification. Key demand-side indicators include the number of approved therapies, manufacturing capacity expansions, and investments in CDMOs specializing in CGT. The need for tubing that can withstand cryopreservation and rapid fluid transfer will drive innovation in product design. Current trend: Fastest-growing segment, expanding at over 10% annually.
Major trends:
Rising adoption of closed-system processing in CGT manufacturing, Increasing demand for custom tubing assemblies with connectors, Growth of CDMOs offering CGT manufacturing services, and Development of tubing materials with enhanced cryoresistance.
Representative participants:
Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, Watson-Marlow Fluid Technology Group, Cole-Parmer, Masterflex, and Thermo Fisher Scientific.
Research and Development (estimated share: 15%)
In R&D settings, silicone tubing is used for lab-scale bioprocessing, media preparation, and analytical workflows. The segment is supported by ongoing investments in pharmaceutical R&D, particularly in early-stage drug development and process optimization. Researchers require flexible, sterilizable tubing that can be easily connected to pumps and instruments, making silicone a preferred choice. The trend toward automation and high-throughput screening is increasing the demand for precision tubing with consistent dimensions and low extractables. Through 2035, the segment will grow in line with global R&D spending, which is expected to rise as biopharma companies invest in novel modalities such as mRNA and peptide therapeutics. The demand for tubing that is compatible with a wide range of solvents and biological fluids will drive product innovation. Additionally, the increasing use of single-use technologies in process development is boosting the consumption of silicone tubing in pilot plants and scale-up studies. Current trend: Stable growth, driven by laboratory automation and process development.
Major trends:
Automation of laboratory processes increasing demand for precision tubing, Growing use of single-use technologies in process development, Expansion of R&D activities in emerging biopharma hubs, and Demand for tubing with documented biocompatibility for regulatory submissions.
Representative participants:
Cole-Parmer, Masterflex, Saint-Gobain, Thermo Fisher Scientific, and Elkem.
Quality Control and Release Testing (estimated share: 10%)
Quality control (QC) and release testing require silicone tubing for sampling, transfer of test materials, and stability studies. The segment is driven by the need for reliable, contamination-free fluid handling in analytical laboratories. Silicone tubing is used in HPLC, dissolution testing, and microbial analysis, where inertness and low extractables are essential. The increasing stringency of regulatory standards, such as USP and EP, is pushing QC laboratories to adopt high-quality tubing with comprehensive documentation. Through 2035, the segment will grow as biopharma companies expand their QC capabilities to support new product launches and ongoing batch release. The demand for tubing that can withstand repeated sterilization cycles and aggressive solvents will drive product development. Additionally, the trend toward continuous quality monitoring and real-time release testing may increase the use of integrated tubing systems with sensors and flow cells. Current trend: Moderate growth, aligned with regulatory compliance requirements.
Major trends:
Increasing regulatory scrutiny on extractables and leachables in QC processes, Adoption of single-use sampling systems to reduce cross-contamination, Growth of contract testing laboratories, and Demand for tubing with validated cleanliness and low particulate levels.
Representative participants:
Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cole-Parmer, Saint-Gobain, Parker Hannifin, and Freudenberg Medical.
Aseptic Filling and Sampling (estimated share: 10%)
Aseptic filling and sampling applications require silicone tubing that can maintain sterility during drug product filling and in-process sampling. The segment is driven by the increasing production of sterile injectables, including biologics, vaccines, and small molecule drugs. Silicone tubing is used in peristaltic pumps for filling, as well as in sampling systems to monitor process parameters without compromising sterility. The demand for tubing assemblies with pre-sterilized connectors and clamps is rising, as manufacturers seek to reduce contamination risks and improve operational efficiency. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from the growth of contract manufacturing organizations (CDMOs) and the expansion of aseptic filling capacity, particularly in emerging markets. Key demand-side indicators include the number of new aseptic filling lines, regulatory approvals for sterile products, and investments in barrier isolator technology. The need for tubing that can withstand gamma irradiation and autoclaving will remain critical. Current trend: Growing with the expansion of aseptic manufacturing lines.
Major trends:
Increasing adoption of ready-to-use sterile tubing assemblies, Growth of CDMOs offering aseptic filling services, Expansion of vaccine production and sterile injectable manufacturing, and Demand for tubing with validated sterilization compatibility.
Representative participants:
Saint-Gobain, Watson-Marlow, Masterflex, Parker Hannifin, and Thermo Fisher Scientific.

Regional Dynamics
Asia-Pacific (estimated share: 35%)
Asia-Pacific is expected to witness the highest growth rate, driven by expanding biopharmaceutical manufacturing in China, India, and Southeast Asia. Increasing investments in single-use technologies and local production of biologics are boosting demand for silicone tubing. The region's large patient population and rising healthcare expenditure further support market expansion. Direction: Fastest-growing region.
North America (estimated share: 30%)
North America remains a major market, supported by a strong biopharma sector and early adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies. The presence of key players and stringent regulatory standards drive demand for high-quality silicone tubing. Growth is sustained by ongoing investments in cell and gene therapy and continuous manufacturing. Direction: Steady growth.
Europe (estimated share: 25%)
Europe holds a significant share, with well-established biopharma clusters in Germany, Switzerland, and the UK. The region's focus on regulatory compliance and quality assurance supports demand for premium silicone tubing. Growth is moderate but steady, with increasing adoption of single-use systems in bioprocessing. Direction: Moderate growth.
Latin America (estimated share: 5%)
Latin America is an emerging market, with Brazil and Mexico leading in biopharmaceutical production. The region is witnessing gradual adoption of single-use technologies, driven by cost pressures and the need for flexible manufacturing. Market growth is supported by government initiatives to boost local drug production. Direction: Emerging growth.
Middle East & Africa (estimated share: 5%)
The Middle East and Africa region is at an early stage of biopharmaceutical development, with investments in healthcare infrastructure and local manufacturing. Demand for silicone tubing is limited but growing, particularly in countries like Saudi Arabia and South Africa. The market is expected to expand as regional biopharma capabilities develop. Direction: Slow but steady growth.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: FSS launches briefings to enforce Korea biotech disclosure reforms - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
Pharma Industry.content:
A view of the Financial Supervisory Service in Yeouido, Seoul./Courtesy of News1
The Financial Supervisory Service said on the 24th that it will hold briefings four times next month for each group of market participants so that the plan to improve disclosures for pharmaceutical and biotech companies can take root in the market early.
To tailor guidance to the characteristics of each market participant, it plans to hold four sessions: ▲ KOSDAQ-listed companies (Sept. 1) ▲ underwriters (Sept. 8) ▲ companies preparing to list (Sept. 15) ▲ main board–listed companies (Sept. 21).
Earlier, on the 30th of last month, the Financial Supervisory Service announced the "comprehensive plan to improve disclosures for pharmaceutical and biotech companies" and required that, when preparing a securities registration statement, the basis for offering price calculation—such as market size, probability of clinical success, approval and review risks, and development period and expense—be specified. It also expanded the scope of disclosures on the size and structure of technology transfer contracts to enhance investor convenience.
At the briefings, the Financial Supervisory Service will present detailed standards for key assumptions used to calculate offering prices in connection with financing. It will also provide guidance on specific application methods for the newly introduced disclosure standards related to periodic and ad hoc disclosures and media reports.
The Financial Supervisory Service said, "We ask for the active interest and participation of corporations and those in charge of disclosures," adding, "The disclosure guidelines presented at the briefings will be posted on our website later."

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Indian pharma has little reason to fear Trump - The Economic Times
Pharma Industry.content:
ANI
Trump tariff impact on Indian pharma industry
Indian pharmaceutical firms have spent decades supplying American patients with affordable medicines. That dominance will be difficult to challenge, despite President Donald Trump’s threat to impose steep tariffs on imported
generic drugs
.
His pledge last month to apply a 100% levy on companies making
off-patent medications
by 2028 (rising to 200% a year later) unless they move production to the US faces formidable commercial and political obstacles. Instead of rushing to fire up new manufacturing facilities, the likes of
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd.
and
Dr. Reddy's Laboratories Ltd.
would be better off biding their time. The duties may never fully materialize.
Also read:
Udan vs Udaan: Delhi court restrains pharmaceutical firm from using 'Udaan' mark
That’s because generic medicines play a crucial role in the
healthcare system
. Once patent protections on branded drugs expire, other manufacturers can produce equivalent versions, introducing competition that drives prices sharply lower. The difference can be enormous. According to one US Food & Drug Administration study, the price of an HIV medicine, Truvada, fell from about $50 to $3 a tablet shortly after generic versions became available.
Bloomberg
Generics account for most US prescriptions
Generic drugmakers operate on high volumes and low margins. Asia’s five-biggest players have an average EBITDA margin, a measure of operating profitability, of around 22%, considerably less than the world’s top five innovative drugmakers. That reflects the economics of a business in which off-patent medicines account for more than 90% of US prescriptions but only a fraction of spending as they are so cheap. With less profit at stake, manufacturers have little incentive to shift production to the US — and no room to absorb tariffs.
Live Events
Bloomberg
India dominates the region's generic medicine producers
That means the levies, if imposed, could be borne by American patients and the wider healthcare system, and ultimately feed into already stubbornly high inflation. Spencer Perlman, a healthcare analyst at Veda Partners, a consultancy firm based in Bethesda, Maryland, estimates that the threatened tariffs could increase total prescription-drug spending by roughly 8% to 15%.
And if the extra cost can’t be passed on to patients, some drugs could become unprofitable to produce, potentially leading to shortages — an even less acceptable trade-off than higher prices. A policy that would make the cheapest medicines much more expensive or unavailable would be politically unpalatable in 2028, a presidential election year.
Also read:
India pharma sector to miss 2030 sales target amid tariff and shipping woes, trade body says
There’s another reason why Indian drugmakers should resist the pressure to set up manufacturing in the US. Recent history hardly makes a compelling case for investing there. Consider Dr. Reddy’s. In March last year, it shut a generic-drug factory in Shreveport, Louisiana, after years of losses. The plant, which had produced medicines including ibuprofen and aspirin, lacked a “clear path to profitability,” a spokesperson told a local newspaper.
For years, the generics trade had been moving out of the US. India's industry was born out of a 1970 decision to abolish pharmaceutical product patents, which encouraged domestic companies to master the art of reverse-engineering Western medicines. By the time India restored product patents in 2005, those companies had spent three decades building the expertise and scale that allowed them to pivot toward off-patent drugs for export. America's own embrace of generics came after a 1984 law opened the door for the FDA to approve the drugs on a shorter timeline, ultimately turning India into the pharmacy of the world.
Bloomberg
India is top source of generic pills to the US
To be sure, some Indian firms have invested in US manufacturing as part of a push into higher-margin treatments. Sun Pharmaceutical, India’s largest drugmaker, and Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. have separately announced such investments. But these are commercial decisions intended to improve profitability, not responses to the threat of tariffs.
Washington has legitimate reasons to worry about relying so heavily on overseas suppliers for essential drugs. But levies are an unusually blunt way of addressing that vulnerability. If the goal is greater resilience, then targeted incentives for strategically important medicines, diversified supply chains and guaranteed purchasing contracts would attack the problem more directly than taxing every imported generic.
The US spent four decades building a system that rewarded whoever could supply safe medicines most cheaply, and Asian companies became extraordinarily good at it. Until Washington proves it’s genuinely willing to undo all that, Indian drugmakers have little reason to panic.

(FDF) manufacturing plant was inspected from August 17 to August 21 and has been issued a Form 483 with four observations.

Pharma Industry.content:
Agencies
Udan vs Udaan: Delhi court restrains pharmaceutical firm from using 'Udaan' mark
New Delhi: A Delhi court has permanently restrained a Hyderabad-based pharmaceutical company from using the trademark 'Udaan' or any similar mark, ruling that it was a clear violation of the rights of consumer goods major
RSPL Health Private Limited
, which had earlier registered its mark 'Udan.'
District Judge Pankaj Sharma, in an ex parte judgment dated August 13, held that the defendant,
Sainus Pharmaceutical Private Limited
, used the mark 'Udaan' in a manner that was "identical and deceptively similar" to the plaintiff's (RSPL's) registered trademark 'Udan'.
The court noted that, according to RSPL Health, known for brands like 'Ghari' detergent, it had adopted the trademark or label Udan with respect to the goods and business of sanitary napkins in 2007 and Sainus Pharma's Udaan mark had infringed its proprietary rights in the said trademark.
"The defendant (Sainus) is not only making the retail sales but is also supplying the impugned goods bearing the impugned trade marks to various other dealers/shopkeepers/retailers in New Delhi, who are making the clandestine and surreptitious sales thereof to the ultimate unwary consumers in the markets of New Delhi viz. Parliament Street, Connaught Place, Barakhamba, Chanakyapuri, Gole Market, Bengali Market etc," RSPL said.
In its order, the court said that the defendant did not appear before it, and thus the plaintiff's contentions remain unrebutted, unchallenged, and uncontroverted.
Live Events
"The plaintiff has established that the defendant has infringed the said trademark and has also committed passing off of goods. Therefore, there is no doubt that the plaintiff is entitled to relief of permanent injunction against the defendant for using the trademark 'Udaan' or any other mark identical or deceptively similar to the word mark, label of plaintiff's trademark Udan," the court said.
Besides the permanent injunction, the court ordered that all seized counterfeit products and infringing materials, including packaging, dies, and blocks bearing the falsified mark, be delivered to RSPL Health for destruction.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: FSS to Hold Pharma-Bio Disclosure Briefings Next Month - Seoul Economic Daily
Pharma Industry.content:
Yonhap News
The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) will hold briefings on its comprehensive plan to improve pharmaceutical and biotech disclosures for listed companies, IPO underwriters and firms preparing to go public.
The FSS said on the 24th that it will hold a series of tailored briefings for each type of market participant starting next month, explaining the background of the plan, its main improvements, and specific methods and cautions for preparing disclosures.
The sessions run in order: KOSDAQ-listed companies on September 1 (Korea Exchange), listing underwriters on September 8 (Korea Institute of Financial Investment), IPO-preparing firms on September 15 (Korea Institute of Financial Investment), and KOSPI-listed companies on September 21 (FSS). Companies and disclosure officers who wish to attend in person can apply through the association hosting each session.
The FSS said it will thoroughly explain the details of each guideline item so that pharmaceutical and biotech firms can fully understand the improved disclosure standards and raise the quality of the information they provide. By preventing incomplete disclosure filings, it aims to minimize the administrative burden on companies and delays in their fundraising schedules.
Earlier, on the 30th of last month, the FSS announced its "Comprehensive Plan to Improve Pharmaceutical and Biotech Disclosures," which centers on standardizing key information used to value companies and requiring more specific disclosure of the details of technology transfer agreements.
Under the plan, pharmaceutical and biotech firms must explain their key assumptions in a standardized format, including the expected market size, the probability of clinical trial success, approval and review risks, and development timelines and costs. For technology transfer agreements, firms are required to disclose details such as upfront payments, development milestones, approval and sales milestones, and royalties.

Symbiotec Pharmalab’s Rs 1,757 crore IPO opens with GMP hinting at 41% upside. Should you bid?
ETMarkets.com
Symbiotec Pharmalab IPO GMP, Listing Date
Synopsis
Symbiotec Pharmalab IPO GMP: Symbiotec Pharmalab’s Rs 1,757 crore IPO opened August 24, with a Rs 938–988 price band and 41% grey-market premium. The issue combines fresh shares and an OFS, while proceeds will partly repay debt. Its specialised API manufacturing, regulatory approvals and biotechnology capabilities offer investors exposure to India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing growth.

Ritesh Presswala

The much-awaited
Symbiotec Pharmalab IPO
opened for subscription, August 24, 2026, with strong grey-market sentiment setting the stage for investor interest. The issue is currently commanding a
GMP
of around 41%, signalling expectations of a potentially strong listing gain.
ADVERTISEMENT
The biopharmaceutical and biotechnology company is looking to raise Rs 1,757 crore through the public issue. The
IPO
comprises a fresh issue of 15 lakh shares worth Rs 150 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of 1.63 crore shares aggregating to Rs 1,607 crore.
The company has fixed the IPO price band at Rs 938–Rs 988 per share.
The IPO will remain open for three days, from August 24 to August 27, 2026. Investors can bid for a minimum of 15 shares, with subsequent bids in multiples of 15. At the upper end of the price band, the minimum investment works out to Rs 14,820.
The shares are proposed to be listed on both the BSE and NSE, with the tentative listing date set for September 1, 2026. IPO allotment is expected to be finalised on August 28, 2026.
The issue is being managed by
JM Financial
, Avendus Capital, Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors and Nomura Financial, while MUFG Intime India Pvt. Ltd. is acting as the registrar.

Symbiotec Pharmalab IPO GMP Today
Symbiotec Pharmalab IPO is currently commanding a GMP of Rs 409, or 41%, against the upper price band of Rs 988 per share. Based on the prevailing grey market premium, the IPO’s estimated listing price stands at around Rs 1,397 per share.
ADVERTISEMENT
ADVERTISEMENT
Valuation under the spotlight
Symbiotec Pharmalab’s IPO valuation is likely to attract close attention from investors. Based on diluted earnings per share for fiscal 2026, the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 49.37 times at the lower end of the price band and rises to 52.00 times at the upper end.
The company’s weighted average return on net worth for the last three financial years was 10.99%.
ADVERTISEMENT
With the IPO price band translating to 469 times the face value at the floor price and 494 times at the cap price, the issue is positioned as a premium offering in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology space.
Where will the IPO proceeds go?
The
Symbiotec Pharmalab
IPO plans to channel Rs 112.50 crore towards the prepayment and/or repayment, fully or partially, of select outstanding borrowings, helping strengthen the company’s balance sheet and potentially reduce its debt burden.
ADVERTISEMENT
The remaining proceeds will be allocated towards general corporate purposes, providing Symbiotec Pharmalab with greater financial flexibility to support its ongoing operations and future business needs.

Skyways Air IPO opens today; GMP at 23%: Key details. Should you subscribe?
About Symbiotec Pharmalab
Founded in 2002, Symbiotec Pharmalab operates across the biopharmaceutical and biotechnology space, developing and manufacturing active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), nutritional ingredients and specialised products for domestic and international markets.
The company’s journey began with laboratory-scale manufacturing of steroidal-hormone APIs in 1995. Over the years, it has expanded into an industrial-scale, backward-integrated manufacturing platform serving the pharmaceutical, nutraceutical and wellness sectors.
Research-driven manufacturing, quality and sustainability form key elements of its business strategy. Its manufacturing operations have also secured approvals and certifications from several international regulatory bodies, including the US FDA, EU-GMP authorities and South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
As of June 30, 2025, Symbiotec Pharmalab operated two industrial-scale API manufacturing plants. Together, these facilities had a maximum capacity of 584.67 metric tonnes (MT) for chemical synthesis and 300 kilolitres of fermentation capacity.
The combination of backward integration, specialised API capabilities and international regulatory approvals gives the company an established position in a segment where manufacturing quality and regulatory compliance can be critical differentiators.
Should you subscribe?
The IPO presents an interesting combination of strong grey-market sentiment, specialised manufacturing capabilities, and exposure to growing pharmaceutical markets.
According to a report by Master Capital Services Ltd.,"The global API market was valued at around USD 305.5 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 424.6 billion by 2030, growing at a 6.8% CAGR. Small-molecule APIs continue to dominate, while biologics are gaining share. The CDMO market is also expected to grow strongly at an 8.2% CAGR, supported by India’s cost advantages and manufacturing capabilities."
The report further stated that Symbiotec Pharmalab provides exposure to specialised pharmaceutical manufacturing, with capabilities in corticosteroid and steroidal-hormone APIs, CDMO services and complex injectables. Its key strength is vertical integration across chemistry, biotechnology and regulated manufacturing. The IPO could offer a potential long-term investment opportunity, according to the report.
